learn.content:
The country’s ledger with the rest of the world

Just as a firm keeps accounts, so does a country. The balance of payments (BoP) is the summary statement of all monetary transactions between a country’s residents and the rest of the world over one year. It is organised into two main accounts:

  • Current account — the "income statement" of trade: goods, services, primary income (wages, dividends, interest on cross-border investment) and secondary income (transfers with no quid pro quo — pensions, aid, gifts).
  • Financial account — the "capital" side: direct investment, portfolio investment, other investment and financial derivatives (the cross-border movement of assets and liabilities).

The BoP always balances to zero

Together with the change in official reserves, the whole balance of payments sums to zero. The deep implication: a current-account deficit must be financed by capital inflows (borrowing from or selling assets to the rest of the world), and a surplus means lending to it. The two accounts are mirror images.

The tourism (travel) balance — the line that matters most here

Within the services account sits the travel (tourism) balance, defined exactly like any trade balance — income minus expenditure:

\[ \text{Travel balance} = \underbrace{\text{income from foreign tourists}}_{\text{export, inflow}} - \underbrace{\text{spending of residents abroad}}_{\text{import, outflow}} \]

Spending by foreigners in the country is an export (a foreign-exchange inflow); spending by residents abroad is an import (an outflow). A surplus marks a tourist-receptive country; a deficit a tourist-emitting one.

Why this is central for Croatia: the country runs a large, persistent deficit in the goods trade (it imports more merchandise than it exports). What keeps the current account afloat is the huge travel surplus — foreign tourists bring in foreign exchange that offsets the goods deficit. Tourism is, quite literally, the line item that balances the national accounts.

Capital flows and the BP curve

Capital chases returns. Net capital export \(K\) (capital leaving minus capital entering) falls as the domestic interest rate rises — a higher \(r\) attracts foreign capital in:

\[ K = f(r), \qquad \frac{dK}{dr} < 0 \]

This creates an indirect link from interest rates to trade: a higher \(r\) → capital inflows → higher demand for the domestic currency → the currency appreciates → exports fall, imports rise → the trade balance deteriorates. The BP curve collects all combinations of output \(Y\) and interest rate \(r\) for which the balance of payments is in equilibrium (\(BP = 0\)); points below it are deficits, points above surpluses.

Internal and external balance are interdependent

Internal balance is goods + money market equilibrium (IS = LM); external balance is a point on the BP curve. They do not move independently. A balance-of-payments deficit drains official reserves, which shrinks the money supply, shifts LM left and raises the interest rate; the higher rate cuts output and imports, nudging the external balance back toward zero. Left alone, the system tends to grind toward simultaneous internal and external balance.

flashcards.question: What is the single thread linking the whole macro course?
flashcards.answer:
The same variables (Y, u, π, i) are looked at over three horizons:
• SHORT run — output is set by DEMAND (Goods, Financial, IS-LM markets).
• MEDIUM run — output returns to its NATURAL level set by SUPPLY (the labour market, AS-AD).
• LONG run — the natural level itself GROWS through capital, human capital and technology.
flashcards.explanation: Demand moves output around a supply-determined trend that itself grows over time.

flashcards.question: Collect the key equilibrium conditions of the course in one place.
flashcards.answer: Goods market: \( Y = Z \). Money market: \( M^s = M^d \). IS-LM: IS \(\cap\) LM. Labour market: \( F(u_n,z)=\dfrac{1}{1+\mu} \). Medium run: \( P=P^e \Rightarrow Y=Y_n \). Open economy / external balance: trade balance = net capital flows (BP = 0).

flashcards.question: Three ways to express GDP — and the expenditure identity.
flashcards.answer:
Production = expenditure = income (all equal). The expenditure identity is
\( Y = C + I + G + (X - IM) \),
and the saving–investment identity is \( S - I = (G + TR - T) + NX \).

flashcards.question: How do you compute the multiplier in the closed and the open economy?
flashcards.answer: Closed: \( \dfrac{1}{1 - c_1} \). Open (with tax rate t and marginal propensity to import m): \( \dfrac{1}{1 - \beta(1-t) + m} \). Both taxes and imports SHRINK the multiplier because they leak demand out of the income–spending loop.

flashcards.question: How do fiscal and monetary policy each move output and the interest rate (IS-LM)?
flashcards.answer: Fiscal expansion (↑G or ↓T) shifts IS right → \(Y\uparrow,\ i\uparrow\). Monetary expansion (↑M) shifts LM down → \(Y\uparrow,\ i\downarrow\). A policy mix combines them to hit both output and the interest rate.

flashcards.question: How is the medium-run equilibrium reached after a demand boom?
flashcards.answer: A demand boom pushes \(Y > Y_n\), so \(u < u_n\); wages and prices rise above expectations (\(P > P^e\)). Expectations adjust up, the AS curve shifts up, and output falls back to \(Y_n\) at a higher price level. Demand affects output only temporarily.

flashcards.question: What determines the natural rate of unemployment and the natural level of output?
flashcards.answer: From wage setting \(=\) price setting: \( F(u_n,z)=\dfrac{1}{1+\mu} \Rightarrow u_n = 1 - \dfrac{1}{1+\mu} + z \). Then \( Y_n = L(1-u_n) \). A higher markup μ or higher z (benefits/protection) raises \(u_n\) and lowers \(Y_n\).

flashcards.question: What ultimately drives long-run growth, and why is capital not enough?
flashcards.answer: Capital accumulation (saving) raises the LEVEL of output per worker, but diminishing returns mean its contribution to the long-run growth rate is zero. SUSTAINED growth requires sustained TECHNOLOGICAL PROGRESS (R&D, human capital).

flashcards.question: Why is the real interest rate the one that matters, and how is it found?
flashcards.answer: Decisions depend on the purchasing-power cost of borrowing/saving, not the money cost. \( r \approx i - \pi^e \). Expectations of future income, profits and real rates shift the IS curve — optimism raises current output.

flashcards.question: How does an open economy change the picture (exchange rate, NX, BoP)?
flashcards.answer: Output equals demand for domestic goods \( Y = C + I + G + NX \), \(NX = X - IM\). A real depreciation raises NX if Marshall-Lerner holds; higher domestic output or a real appreciation lowers NX. The balance of payments (current + financial account) must balance: a current-account deficit is financed by capital inflows.

flashcards.question: Why is the tourism (travel) balance central for a country like Croatia?
flashcards.answer: Travel = income from foreign tourists (export/inflow) − spending of residents abroad (import/outflow). A surplus marks a tourist-receptive country. For Croatia, the large travel surplus typically offsets the persistent goods-trade deficit, supporting the current account.

flashcards.question: Connect Okun’s law and the Phillips curve to the rest of the model.
flashcards.answer: Okun’s law links output growth to changes in unemployment (above-trend growth lowers u). The Phillips curve links low unemployment to higher inflation. Together they tie the demand side (Y) to the labour market (u) and to prices (π) — the same chain the AS curve formalizes.

learn.content:
Final Exam Roadmap — the whole of macro on one page

The course follows the same variables — output \(Y\), unemployment \(u\), inflation \(\pi\), the interest rate \(i\) — across three horizons. In the short run demand rules; in the medium run output returns to a supply-determined natural level; in the long run that level grows. Drill the per-topic categories in this lesson, then use this set to connect them.

\[ \begin{aligned}\text{GDP identity:}\quad & Y = C + I + G + (X - IM)\\[2pt]\text{Goods-market multiplier:}\quad & \frac{1}{1 - c_1}\;\; \Big(\text{open: } \tfrac{1}{1-\beta(1-t)+m}\Big)\\[2pt]\text{Money market:}\quad & M = \$Y\,L(i)\\[2pt]\text{Natural rate:}\quad & u_n = 1 - \frac{1}{1+\mu} + z\\[2pt]\text{Medium run:}\quad & P = P^e \;\Rightarrow\; Y = Y_n\\[2pt]\text{Real interest rate:}\quad & r \approx i - \pi^e\\[2pt]\text{External balance:}\quad & NX = X - IM,\;\; BP = 0\end{aligned} \]

First midterm (Intro + L2–L5)

  • Fundamentals: objectives, variables, fiscal/monetary/income policy, the three horizons.
  • Unemployment & inflation: \(L = E + U\), CPI, real vs nominal rates, Okun’s law, the Phillips curve.
  • GDP: nominal/real/potential, the deflator, the GDP gap, growth rates, per capita.
  • National accounts: three approaches, the models \(Y=C+I+G+NX\), value added, NACE.
  • Goods market: \(C = c_0 + c_1 Y_D\), equilibrium \(Y = Z\), the multiplier.
  • Financial markets: \(M^d = \$Y\,L(i)\), \(M^s = M^d\), bonds, open-market operations.
  • IS-LM: IS (goods) ∩ LM (money), fiscal + monetary policy, the policy mix.

Second midterm (Ch6 + AS-AD + Long Run + Expectations + Open Economy)

  • Labour market: WS \(W = P^e F(u,z)\), PS \(P = (1+\mu)W\), natural rate \(u_n\), natural output \(Y_n\).
  • AS-AD (medium run): AS up (labour market), AD down (IS-LM); \(P = P^e \Rightarrow Y = Y_n\).
  • Long run / growth: \(Y = F(K, N)\), diminishing returns, Solow saving, technology, human capital, convergence.
  • Expectations: Fisher \(r \approx i - \pi^e\), present value, expectations in the IS relation.
  • Open economy — trade: import function \(IM = IM_0 + mY\), open multiplier, the exchange rate, NX, Marshall-Lerner.
  • Balance of payments: current + financial account, the tourism balance, \(K = f(r)\), the BP curve, internal/external balance.

Exam strategy

Closed questions reward exact conditions and formulas (the multiplier, \(u_n\), \(r \approx i - \pi^e\), \(NX = X - IM\)). Open questions reward concept + mechanism ("a fiscal expansion shifts IS right → Y and i rise; in an open economy imports rise, so NX falls"). Anchor one formula per topic, then trace the chain demand → labour market → prices → external sector.

One sentence for the whole course: aggregate demand moves output around a supply-determined natural level in the short and medium run, while technological progress lifts that natural level in the long run.
